source: Maglio & Kirsh (1996) Epistemic action increases with skill
finding: Two Tetris learners practised about 20 hours each. Extra actions that are later undone (backtracking) went up with skill, not down. Kirsh and Maglio 1994 could not show this; this paper does.
numbers: 2 players, ~20 h each, ~40,000 keystrokes. Extra rotations occurred in 4% (beginner), 5% (intermediate), 7% (expert) of episodes for player LA (p<.01); mean about 0.2 extra rotations per episode. Slow-speed episodes only.
limits: Only 2 participants, one game. Extra rotations are a minority of actions. Not a controlled experiment; skill and game speed are confounded (handled by using only slow episodes).
agent_relevance: Experts do not think less in the world. A scaffold should expect skilled use to include more write-and-revise steps, not fewer, and should not penalise them as waste.

source: Maglio & Kirsh (1996) Epistemic action increases with skill - speed
finding: Despite more backtracking, speed still followed the power law of practice. Power curves fit better than line or exponential for all three timing measures in both players.
numbers: Time between actions, power-fit r2 .91 (LA) and .96 (TM) vs linear .77 and .81; time to place a zoid power r2 .83 and .85 vs linear .77 and .68.
limits: Two players only. Shows extra actions are compatible with efficiency; does not itself show the actions cause the speed.
agent_relevance: Extra external steps can coexist with faster overall performance: judge a scaffold by total time and accuracy, not step count.

source: Maglio & Kirsh (1996) - early rotations as decision aid
finding: Extra rotations came early in an episode, 400-500 ms before the piece reached its final orientation, and not after errors. The authors read them as information-gathering, not motor mistakes. A mirror-image check ruled out simple perceptual error.
numbers: Mean time to reach target orientation when extra rotations occurred: 676 ms (SD 149) for one zoid type and 754 ms (SD 296) for others; with no extra rotations about 1122-1127 ms. Significant (t198=2.82, p<.005 for one type).
limits: Correlational, from log data. Rival reading (habit, impatience) is not fully removed; no manipulation of the rotate key.
agent_relevance: Support for a design rule: take a cheap reversible action early to see something, then decide.

source: Berry (2023) No Next Box, No Experts: epistemic sampling in extreme Tetris expertise
finding: At a special tournament the Next Box (preview of the next piece) was hidden. Elite players could not score a single Tetris. The author argues experts rely on sampling the world (the preview) rather than on epistemic rotation, which they have too little time for.
numbers: 11 players compared in both tournaments; paired t tests all t>4.5, p<.001. Most lines cleared: about 130-230 in the normal tournament vs 4-36 with no preview (table text is jumbled in the PDF, ranges read by eye). No-preview high scores 3,420 to 30,800.
limits: One-off case study, observational; hiding the preview changes game strategy as well as information, so the effect cannot be pinned to information alone. A rival to the 1994/1996 rotation account.
agent_relevance: Extra external information about the near future may matter more to experts than moves that test options. A scaffold should keep a visible look-ahead (plan, next steps) in view.

source: Cook, Yip & Goldin-Meadow (2012) Gestures, but not meaningless movements, lighten working memory load
finding: Adults who gestured while explaining a factoring solution recalled more letters than adults told to keep still or to move their hands in meaningless circles. So meaningful movement, not movement as such, helps.
numbers: N=115 (16 more excluded for gesturing in no-gesture trials). Each person did 2 of 3 conditions, 15 problems each. Meaningless vs Meaningful beta=-.17, z=3.23, p<.01. No movement vs Meaningful beta=-.13, z=2.61, p<.01.
limits: First-condition-only check: meaningless p=.057 (n.s.), no-movement p=.02. With verbal controls: meaningless p=.079. Gesture was instructed; one math task; mostly pointing gestures; no effect size reported. Page read via fetch summary.
agent_relevance: Offloading worked here only for movement tied to meaning. For an agent: externalising must be about the task content; filler writing does not count.

source: Overoye & Wilson (2020) Does gesture lighten the load? The case of verbal analogies
finding: A conceptual extension and partial reversal. With verbal analogies, people remembered MORE digits when told not to gesture than when told to gesture. This is the opposite of the math findings.
numbers: N=44 recruited, 40 analysed. Proportion recalled 0.42 (no gesture) vs 0.39 (gesture), t(39)=2.15, p=.04, d=0.34; F(1,38)=4.93, p=.03. Experiment 1b: 0.38 vs 0.33, t(20)=2.16, p=.04, d=0.47.
limits: Small samples, p near .04, instructed gesture, one task type. Authors say task type and gesture type may matter. Different task from the original, so not a direct failed replication.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: offloading is not free. Forced externalising can add load on verbal tasks. Do not force a write-out step on every task.

source: Dargue, Sweller & Jones (2019) When our hands help us understand: meta-analysis of gesture on comprehension
finding: Across 83 samples, gesture with speech gave a moderate benefit to comprehension. Producing gesture helped much more than watching it.
numbers: Random effects overall d=.61 (95% CI .50-.72), z=11.04. Production d=.91 (CI .64-1.19); observation d=.54 (CI .43-.66). Heterogeneity high (I2 about 67-69%). Preschool d=.73, primary d=.58; adolescents showed no significant benefit.
limits: Comprehension of spoken messages, not directly thinking or problem solving. Mixed designs. High heterogeneity.
agent_relevance: Doing the act yourself beats looking at it: supports having the agent generate its own external trace rather than only read one.

source: Pouw, de Nooijer, van Gog, Zwaan & Paas (2014) Toward a more embedded/extended perspective on the cognitive function of gestures
finding: Theory review. Treats gesture as an external tool that replaces or supports inner steps, like Tetris rotation. Admits gestures are not free and are traded for inner strategies over time.
numbers: Almost no effect sizes in the paper. First 100,000 of 172,225 characters read via fetch.
quote: cognitive processes flow to wherever it is cheaper to perform them
limits: Theory paper, no new data; several predictions untested (wrist weights, mouse speed). Mechanism (proprioceptive vs visual) unresolved.
agent_relevance: Frames a cost-benefit rule an agent could use: externalise when internal cost is high, drop it when learned.

source: Delgado, Gomez & Sarria (2011) via Pouw et al. (2014) - pointing in children's memory
finding: Children aged 2-4 pointed more when they had to remember a location over 45-60 s, even after the table was turned 540 degrees. In ages 4-6, blocking gesture hurt only children who habitually pointed.
numbers: As reported second-hand: delays 45-60 s, rotation 540 degrees. No effect sizes in the secondary source.
limits: Read only through the Pouw et al. summary, not the original.
agent_relevance: Individual differences: the benefit of an external aid depends on whether the user already uses it.

source: Chu et al. (2013) and Marstaller & Burianova (2013) via Pouw et al. (2014)
finding: Lower spatial ability or lower working memory capacity predicted more gesturing. People with low working memory were hurt more when gesture was prohibited.
numbers: No numbers in the secondary source.
limits: Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: Moderator is capacity: the weaker the inner resource, the more the external act helps. Weaker base model, more externalising.

source: Kirsh (2009) tic-tac-toe external grids via Pouw et al. (2014)
finding: Having an external grid helped more on a 4x4 board than on a 3x3 board, and mainly helped people with low spatial ability.
numbers: Board sizes 3x3 vs 4x4. No numerical outcomes in the secondary source.
limits: Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: Support grows with task size: externalise more as the problem grows beyond easy inner capacity.

source: Martin & Schwartz (2005) and Warburton et al. (2013) via Pouw et al. (2014)
finding: Children aged 9-10 learned fractions better with manipulable tiles than with drawings. Dancers who 'marked' a routine (reduced movement) did better than those who rehearsed fully, so movement has its own cost.
numbers: No numbers in the secondary source.
limits: Second-hand only; the dance result is cost-side evidence.
agent_relevance: Manipulable representations beat static ones; a reduced version of an action can be cheaper and still helpful.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) timing claim: rotation about 300 ms vs mental rotation about 1000 ms
finding: A search summary says a physical 90 degree rotation plus button press takes about 300 ms against about 1000 ms for mental rotation.
numbers: ~300 ms vs ~1000 ms (unverified; the original PDF could not be downloaded this session).
limits: From a search summary, not read in the original. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: If true, the external act is about 3 times faster than the inner one; check before citing.

source: Nye et al. (2021) Show your work: scratchpads for intermediate computation
finding: Letting language models write intermediate steps to a scratchpad made them do multi-step computation they failed at in one pass. Without a scratchpad, models fail on longer addition even at the largest tested size.
numbers: Polynomial evaluation: direct 8.8% vs scratchpad 20.1% few-shot; 31.8% vs 50.7% fine-tuned. Python tracing and MBPP execution also improved. Addition trained on 1-8 digits: scratchpad models generalise to 9-10 digits beyond a critical size; baselines do not.
limits: Early LM sizes; needs scratchpad format supervision or a few-shot example; hand-designed trace; absolute accuracies still low on hard tasks.
agent_relevance: Direct base for S2/S4: write intermediate state as an epistemic action. Gains are on mechanical, multi-step tasks.

source: Merrill & Sabharwal (2024) The expressive power of transformers with chain of thought
finding: Proof that scratchpad length sets what a transformer can compute. Without intermediate tokens only a small class (TC0) is reachable. Log-many steps add little; linear steps allow finite-state-machine simulation; polynomial steps reach polynomial-time problems.
numbers: Log steps: contained in L. Linear steps: recognise regular languages (NC1-complete) unless TC0=NC1. Polynomial steps: polynomial-time under stated assumptions.
limits: Theory; idealised transformers; rests on complexity conjectures; says nothing on whether training finds such traces.
agent_relevance: A formal reason to write: the context is the machine's working memory. Steps must scale with problem depth; short notes will not do.

source: Li, Liu, Zhou & Ma (2024) Chain of thought empowers transformers to solve inherently serial problems
finding: Constant-depth transformers with T intermediate steps can express any circuit of size T. Experiments on four serial tasks show a large accuracy gain when CoT is on.
numbers: Tasks: modular addition, permutation composition (S5), iterated squaring, circuit value problem. CoT helps the serial ones; modular addition (parallel) is solved without it.
limits: Synthetic tasks, small transformers trained from scratch, not pre-trained LLMs. Exact table values were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Predicts that serial tasks need external steps and parallel ones do not: choose when to externalise by seriality.

source: Feng et al. (2023) Towards revealing the mystery behind chain of thought
finding: Without CoT, a bounded-size transformer cannot solve arithmetic expressions or linear equations unless size grows super-polynomially; with CoT a constant-size model can. Also shows CoT works for dynamic programming.
numbers: Log-precision transformer; arithmetic and linear equation tasks over finite fields; DP tasks. Experimental accuracies not extracted.
limits: Theory plus synthetic experiments; only the intro and setup sections were read closely.
agent_relevance: The cost of not writing grows with problem size, which is the epistemic action argument in formal form.

source: Pfau, Merrill & Bowman (2024) Let's think dot by dot
finding: Discriminating test between 'content of the steps helps' and 'extra token compute helps'. Small transformers solved 3SUM and 2SUM-Transform with meaningless filler dots, but only with dense supervision. Filler stays inside TC0.
numbers: 3SUM: 100% with filler, fails without. 2SUM-Transform: 94% with filler. Gap rises with input length up to length 12. Learning filler use was hard and varied across 5 runs.
limits: Small Llama (34M) trained from scratch on synthetic tasks. Commercial models did not benefit from filler on QA and math (Claude 2, GPT-3.5 per the paper).
agent_relevance: Some of the gain from writing is raw compute, not meaning. But for natural tasks, meaningful steps are what current models use.

source: Lanham et al. (2023) Measuring faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning
finding: Tested whether the written chain really drives the answer. Truncating, adding mistakes, paraphrasing and replacing with filler dots changed answers very differently by task. Filler gave no gain on the models tested; larger models used the chain less.
numbers: Filler tokens: no accuracy increase on any task, slight drops on TruthfulQA and OpenBookQA. Faithfulness (AOC) varies widely across tasks. Generated mistakes were plausible at least 80% of the time.
limits: One model family; multiple-choice tasks; faithfulness measured by behaviour only.
agent_relevance: The external trace is not always used. A scaffold should check that later steps depend on earlier written steps.

source: Sprague et al. (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus own tests on 20 datasets and 14 models. CoT helps mostly on math and symbolic/logic tasks and little on commonsense or reading tasks.
numbers: Up to 95% of CoT gain on MMLU is on questions with an equals sign in question or output. Little to no gain on CSQA, PIQA, SiQA, WinoGrande, ARC. For math/logic, an external symbolic solver beats CoT for execution.
limits: Mostly prompt-based CoT; models up to Llama 3.1 and GPT-4o era; task categories assigned by authors.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: write-it-out is a symbolic-execution aid. For soft tasks it costs tokens and adds little; for symbolic tasks a tool beats writing.

source: Gao et al. (2023) PAL: Program-aided language models
finding: Let the model write a program as its reasoning and run it with a Python interpreter. This is the strong version of the external act: the world does the computing.
numbers: GSM8K: +15 points absolute over PaLM-540B with CoT. GSM-Hard (large numbers): +40 points. Colored objects +8.8 over CoT; Penguins +14.1; Object counting 96.7% (+23.7); Repeat copy +21.8.
limits: Mathematical and algorithmic tasks with exact computation; Codex-era models; needs code the model can write correctly.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S4 run-code-to-think: delegate exact computation, keep language for decomposition.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Program of Thoughts prompting
finding: Separating computation (interpreter) from reasoning (model) raised accuracy over CoT on math and finance QA in few-shot and zero-shot.
numbers: Average gain over CoT about 12% across 5 math word-problem and 3 financial QA datasets (mainly Codex).
limits: Numerical tasks only; Codex; the figure is from the abstract.
agent_relevance: A second group agrees with PAL: delegating arithmetic is a robust gain.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo & Griffiths (2025) Mind your step (by step)
finding: Used human cases where deliberation hurts. Writing out reasoning also hurt models in 3 of 6 task types.
numbers: Implicit statistical learning: drop up to 36.3 points absolute for o1-preview vs GPT-4o; CoT lowered accuracy in all 6 vision-language models on face recognition; exception-laden labels took up to 331% more iterations to learn.
limits: The other 3 task types showed mixed or no harm. Humans and models are only loosely parallel.
agent_relevance: Failure case for externalising: verbal notes lose perceptual or statistical information. Do not verbalise when the task needs implicit pattern sense.

source: Zeng et al. (2026) The tool-overuse illusion
finding: LLMs call tools when they do not need to. Models misjudge what they know, and unnecessary external actions cost accuracy.
numbers: Average 0.93 unnecessary tool calls per query. Accuracy drops 3.29 to 14.48% on questions answerable from internal knowledge. Qwen3-8B averages 2.2 calls even where avg@1024>0.8. Knowledge-aware DPO cut overuse 82.8% in a 32B model with +3% accuracy; efficiency reward cut tool turns 59.4% (6.83 to 2.77) at 7B.
limits: Preprint; math and QA tool benchmarks; trained-model fixes, not prompt-only.
agent_relevance: The cost side of epistemic action: add a gate asking 'do I need the external step?' before acting.

source: Rios-Garcia et al. (2026) AI scientists produce results without reasoning scientifically
finding: Over 25,000 agent runs in eight domains. Agents do act on the world (run tools), but often do not use what the action returned.
numbers: Base model explains 41.4% of explained variance vs 1.5% for scaffold. Evidence ignored in 68% of traces; beliefs never updated in 71%; refutation-driven revision 26%; untested hypotheses 53% (63% in hypothesis domains); convergent multi-test evidence 7%.
limits: Preprint; science agents; trace labelling by models; authors argue scaffolds alone cannot fix it.
agent_relevance: Epistemic actions only help if the result is read back. The schema needs an explicit step: state what the result changes.
